Apical Diagnosis (AAE).name: Normal Apical Tissues
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).definition: Teeth with normal periapical tissues that are not sensitive to percussion or palpation testing. Lamina dura is intact and PDL space is uniform. Swelling and sinus tract are absent.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).concise_summary: No pain to percussion or palpation; intact lamina dura and uniform periodontal ligament space.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).clinical_definition: The apical tissues are clinically normal. They are not sensitive to percussion or palpation, and the surrounding lamina dura and PDL space are normal.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).main_finding_pattern: No pain to percussion/palpation/biting and normal apical radiograph
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).confirming_findings: Uniform PDL space; intact lamina dura; no swelling or sinus tract.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).patient_symptoms_chief_complaint: No apical symptoms. Patient should not report pain on biting, chewing, percussion, or palpation from apical pathosis.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).percussion: Negative/normal; always compare with adjacent and contralateral teeth.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).bite_test_pressure: Negative/normal; no pain on biting or pressure.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).swelling_sinus_tract_systemic: No swelling, no sinus tract, no suppuration, no fever or lymphadenopathy.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).radiographic_findings: Intact lamina dura, uniform periodontal ligament space, no apical radiolucency or inflammatory radiopacity.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).pulpal_test_context: Can be paired with many pulpal diagnoses, including normal pulp, reversible pulpitis, symptomatic irreversible pulpitis, asymptomatic irreversible pulpitis, necrotic pulp, previously treated, or previously initiated therapy. Pulp tests guide the pulpal diagnosis.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).choose_this_diagnosis_when: Select when periapical tests and radiographs are normal even if the pulp diagnosis is abnormal.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).do_not_confuse_with_note: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis with normal apical tissues can still have thermal pain. The apical diagnosis remains normal if apical tests are normal.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).differentiate_from_common_pitfalls: Do not confuse symptomatic apical periodontitis if the only pain is thermal/sweet pain without percussion, palpation, or biting tenderness. Early symptomatic irreversible pulpitis can still have normal apical tissues.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).treatment_planning_note: Treat according to the pulpal diagnosis/etiology; no apical treatment is needed beyond normal apical tissues.

Apical Diagnosis (AAE).name: Symptomatic Apical Periodontitis
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).definition: Inflammation of apical periodontium producing clinical symptoms including painful response to biting and/or percussion or palpation. Radiograph may be normal, show widened PDL, or radiolucency.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).concise_summary: Pain on biting and/or percussion or palpation; may or may not have apical radiolucency.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).clinical_definition: Inflammation, usually of the apical periodontium, producing clinical symptoms such as pain to biting, percussion, and/or palpation.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).main_finding_pattern: Pain to biting, percussion, and/or palpation; radiograph may be normal or abnormal ("Widened PDL", "Radiolucency")
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).confirming_findings: Reproducible tenderness to percussion, palpation, or bite test.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).patient_symptoms_chief_complaint: Pain or tenderness on biting/chewing; tooth may feel high in care. Pain may be localized by the patient better than pulpal thermal pain.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).percussion: Positive/tender. Severity can range from mild tenderness to severe pain.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).palpation: May be positive/tender over the apex if inflammation extends through cortical bone/periosteum.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).bite_test_pressure: Often positive to biting pressure. Tooth Slooth or customized bite may reproduce the complaint.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).swelling_sinus_tract_systemic: Usually no diffuse swelling or systemic signs. Local tenderness may exist without abscess formation.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).radiographic_findings: May show normal PDL with early, widened PDL, loss of lamina dura, or apical radiolucency depending on disease stage.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).pulpal_test_context: May be associated with vital inflamed pulp, pulp necrosis, previously treated teeth, or previously initiated therapy. Pulp tests determine the paired pulpal diagnosis.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).choose_this_diagnosis_when: Select when the key objective finding is pain to biting/percussion/palpation, with or without radiographic apical changes.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).do_not_confuse_with_note: Acute apical abscess if swelling/pus/systemic signs are present; cracked tooth if bite/release pattern and isolated probing suggest fracture.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).differentiate_from_common_pitfalls: Differentiate from normal apical tissues by tenderness to percussion/palpation/bite. Differentiate from acute apical abscess by absence of pus, swelling, and systemic findings. Also differentiate from cracked tooth or primary periodontal disease.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).treatment_planning_note: Often indicates apical inflammation requiring management of the pulpal/endodontic cause and occlusal evaluation/occlusal reduction when present.

Apical Diagnosis (AAE).name: Asymptomatic Apical Periodontitis
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).definition: Inflammation and destruction of apical periodontium of pulpal origin, appearing as apical radiolucency without clinical symptoms.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).concise_summary: Apical radiolucency/destruction of apical periodontium of pulpal origin, without clinical symptoms.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).clinical_definition: Inflammation and destruction of apical periodontium of pulpal origin, seen radiographically, without clinical symptoms.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).main_finding_pattern: Apical radiolucency but no pain to percussion or palpation
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).confirming_findings: Radiographic apical bone destruction of pulpal origin, clinically asymptomatic.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).patient_symptoms_chief_complaint: No pain. Often discovered incidentally on radiographs.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).swelling_sinus_tract_systemic: No swelling, no sinus tract, no pus, no systemic signs.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).radiographic_findings: Apical radiolucency / osseous destruction of pulpal origin. PDL may be widened and lamina dura may be absent at the apex.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).pulpal_test_context: Usually paired with pulp necrosis or previously treated teeth, but the pulpal/endodontic status must be tested and documented separately.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).choose_this_diagnosis_when: Select when there is an apical radiolucency consistent with pulpal origin but the tooth is asymptomatic to percussion and palpation.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).do_not_confuse_with_note: Chronic apical abscess if a draining sinus tract is present; non-endodontic radiolucencies if pulpal origin is not confirmed.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).differentiate_from_common_pitfalls: Differentiate from chronic apical abscess by absence of a sinus tract/drainage. Differentiate from non-endodontic radiolucencies by confirming pulpal origin, periodontal probing, and anatomy.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).treatment_planning_note: Endodontic treatment/retreatment is indicated according to restorability, pulpal status, and prognosis.

Apical Diagnosis (AAE).name: Chronic Apical Abscess
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).definition: An inflammatory reaction to pulpal infection and necrosis characterized by gradual onset, little or no discomfort, and intermittent discharge of pus through an associated sinus tract. Gutta-percha tracing typically confirms the involved root.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).concise_summary: Gradual onset, little or no discomfort, and intermittent pus discharge through a sinus tract associated with pulpal infection/necrosis.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).clinical_definition: Inflammatory reaction to pulpal infection and necrosis with gradual onset, little or no discomfort, and intermittent pus drainage through an associated sinus tract.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).main_finding_pattern: Sinus tract, parulis, or intermittent drainage with little/no discomfort
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).confirming_findings: Gutta-percha tracing points to involved root/tooth; radiolucency commonly present.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).patient_symptoms_chief_complaint: Little or no pain. Patient may report a 'gum boil', intermittent drainage, bad taste, or recurring swelling that drains.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).percussion: Often normal or mildly tender; can vary.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).palpation: May be normal or mildly tender; palpate for a draining sinus/parulis.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).bite_test_pressure: Usually minimal pain unless acute exacerbation occurs.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).swelling_sinus_tract_systemic: Sinus tract/parulis is the key finding; intermittent purulent drainage may be present. Usually no fever/malaise unless it becomes acute.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).radiographic_findings: Typically apical radiolucency / osseous destruction. Trace a sinus tract with a gutta-percha cone and take a radiograph to identify the source.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).pulpal_test_context: Usually associated with pulp necrosis or a previously treated tooth with persistent/recurrent infection.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).choose_this_diagnosis_when: Select when a draining sinus tract or intermittent pus discharge is present and the source traces to the involved tooth.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).do_not_confuse_with_note: Periodontal abscess, vertical root fracture, or acute apical abscess with active swelling/pain.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).differentiate_from_common_pitfalls: Differentiate from asymptomatic apical periodontitis by sinus tract/drainage. Differentiate from periodontal abscess by periodontal probing pattern and sinus tract tracing. Differentiate from acute apical abscess by gradual onset and minimal pain.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).treatment_planning_note: Trace the sinus tract before treatment whenever possible; treat the infected root canal system or consider retreatment/surgery/extraction depending on restorability and prognosis.

Apical Diagnosis (AAE).name: Acute Apical Abscess
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).definition: An inflammatory reaction to pulpal infection and necrosis characterized by rapid onset, spontaneous pain, tenderness of tooth to pressure, pus formation, and swelling of associated tissues.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).concise_summary: Rapid onset, spontaneous pain, tenderness to pressure, pus formation, and swelling associated with pulpal infection/necrosis.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).clinical_definition: Inflammatory reaction to pulpal infection and necrosis with rapid onset, spontaneous pain, extreme tenderness to pressure, pus formation, and swelling of associated tissues.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).main_finding_pattern: Rapid onset spontaneous pain + swelling/pus + extreme tenderness to pressure
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).confirming_findings: Localized or diffuse swelling; possible fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy; radiograph may be normal early.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).patient_symptoms_chief_complaint: Rapid onset, moderate to severe spontaneous pain; pain on pressure/biting; patient may report swelling.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).percussion: Usually very positive; tooth is extremely tender to pressure/percussion.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).palpation: Often positive with localized or diffuse soft-tissue tenderness/swelling.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).bite_test_pressure: Very painful to bite or touch; tooth may feel elevated/high.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).swelling_sinus_tract_systemic: Swelling and pus formation are key. Fever, malaise, and lymphadenopathy may be present; assess airway/fascial-space risk.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).radiographic_findings: May show no apical radiographic destruction early, or may show widened PDL/apical radiolucency depending on stage.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).pulpal_test_context: Usually associated with pulp necrosis or infected previously treated root canal system.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).choose_this_diagnosis_when: Select when rapid painful swelling/pus is present with severe pressure tenderness, even if the radiograph does not yet show an apical radiolucency.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).do_not_confuse_with_note: Symptomatic apical periodontitis without swelling; chronic apical abscess with a draining sinus and minimal pain.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).differentiate_from_common_pitfalls: Differentiate from symptomatic apical periodontitis by swelling/pus/systemic signs. Differentiate from chronic apical abscess by acute pain, rapid onset, and tissue swelling. Rule out non-endodontic fascial space infections or periodontal abscess.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).treatment_planning_note: Urgency depends on severity/systemic involvement. Manage source of infection, drainage when indicated, analgesia, and medical referral/antibiotics only when systemic signs or spreading infection exist.

Apical Diagnosis (AAE).name: Condensing osteitis
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).definition: Diffuse radiopaque lesion representing a localized bony reaction to a low-grade inflammatory stimulus, usually seen at the apex of tooth with extensive caries or long-standing pulp irritation.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).concise_summary: Diffuse radiopaque lesion at the apex caused by localized bone reaction to low-grade inflammatory stimulus.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).clinical_definition: Diffuse radiopaque lesion representing a localized bony reaction to a low-grade inflammatory stimulus, usually at the tooth apex.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).main_finding_pattern: Periapical radiopacity/sclerosis associated with an endodontic inflammatory source
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).confirming_findings: Diffuse radiopaque apical lesion; often deep caries/large restoration/necrotic or chronically inflamed pulp.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).patient_symptoms_chief_complaint: Symptoms vary; may be asymptomatic, or may have a variety of chronic low-grade pulpal symptoms; can coexist with symptomatic apical periodontitis.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).percussion: May be normal or positive depending on current apical inflammation.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).palpation: May be normal or positive depending on current apical inflammation.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).bite_test_pressure: May be normal or tender if associated with symptomatic apical periodontitis.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).swelling_sinus_tract_systemic: No sinus tract or swelling unless another apical diagnosis/abscess is also present.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).radiographic_findings: Periapical radiopacity/sclerotic bone around the apex, often diffuse. Look for association with deep caries, large restorations, necrosis, or chronic pulpal inflammation.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).pulpal_test_context: Usually associated with chronic pulpal inflammation, pulp necrosis, or a low-grade irritant. Pulp tests guide the paired pulpal diagnosis.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).choose_this_diagnosis_when: Select when the key apical radiographic finding is inflammatory periapical radiopacity rather than radiolucency, and the tooth has an endodontic inflammatory source.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).do_not_confuse_with_note: Idiopathic osteosclerosis, cemento-osseous dysplasia, hypercementosis, anatomic radiopacity.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).differentiate_from_common_pitfalls: Differentiate from idiopathic osteosclerosis, cemento-osseous dysplasia, hypercementosis, condensing bone, or normal anatomic radiopacity. The key is establishing that the lesion is linked to an endodontic inflammatory source.
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).treatment_planning_note: Treat the pulp/endodontic source when indicated; sclerosis may regress partially or completely over time after successful treatment.

Apical Diagnosis (AAE).name: Chronic Apical Periodontitis
Apical Diagnosis (AAE).definition: A longstanding low-grade periapical lesion characterized by radiographic radiolucency and minimal or localized discomfort.

Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).name: Normal Pulp
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).definition: A clinical diagnostic category in which the pulp is symptom-free and normally responsive to pulp testing.
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).required_supporting_findings: Normal response compared with controls; no disease-driving history or signs.
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).what_would_change_diagnosis: Symptoms with cold/sweets would shift toward reversible pulpitis; no response would require necrosis/previously treated evaluation.
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).common_mistake_to_avoid: Calling a tooth normal without testing controls.

Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).name: Reversible Pulpitis
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).definition: A clinical diagnosis based on subjective and objective findings indicating that inflammation should resolve and the pulp return to normal after management of the cause.
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).required_supporting_findings: Provoked pain only; no spontaneous pain; no lingering; identifiable reversible cause.
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).what_would_change_diagnosis: Lingering thermal pain or spontaneous pain shifts to symptomatic irreversible pulpitis.
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).common_mistake_to_avoid: Using pain intensity alone; intensity may be high but still reversible if brief and stimulus-bound.

Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).name: Symptomatic Irreversible Pulpitis
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).definition: A clinical diagnosis indicating a vital inflamed pulp that is incapable of healing; descriptors include lingering thermal pain, spontaneous pain, and referred pain.
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).if_you_find: Lingering cold/heat pain, spontaneous pain, or referred pain in a vital tooth
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).required_supporting_findings: Thermal test reproduces lingering pain; tooth responds to sensibility testing; deep caries/restoration/crack history likely.
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).what_would_change_diagnosis: No response to cold/EPT shifts toward necrosis; no symptoms with exposure/deep caries may be asymptomatic irreversible.
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).common_mistake_to_avoid: Ruling it out because percussion is normal.

Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).name: Asymptomatic Irreversible Pulpitis
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).definition: A clinical diagnosis indicating a vital inflamed pulp incapable of healing, with no clinical symptoms; inflammation is produced by caries, caries excavation, trauma, etc.
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).if_you_find: No symptoms but carious/mechanical/traumatic exposure or deep caries likely to expose the pulp
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).required_supporting_findings: Vital response usually present; no clinical symptoms; clinical finding indicates pulp cannot heal.
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).what_would_change_diagnosis: Brief stimulus pain without exposure and removable cause may be reversible pulpitis.
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).common_mistake_to_avoid: Assuming no pain means no endodontic disease.

Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).name: Pulp Necrosis
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).definition: A clinical diagnostic category indicating death of the dental pulp; the pulp is usually nonresponsive to pulp testing.
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).if_you_find: No response to cold/EPT compared with responsive controls
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).required_supporting_findings: Consistent history/signs: trauma, discoloration, deep caries, previous pulpitis, apical findings, sinus/swelling.
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).what_would_change_diagnosis: Root-filled canals = previously treated; partial therapy = previously initiated; recent trauma/calcification can give false negative.
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).common_mistake_to_avoid: Diagnosing necrosis from one failed cold test without controls.
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).add_apical_diagnosis_based_on: Normal vs symptomatic/asymptomatic apical periodontitis vs abscess vs condensing osteitis.

Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).name: Previously Treated
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).definition: A clinical diagnostic category indicating that the tooth has been endodontically treated and the canals are obturated with filling materials other than intracanal medicaments.
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).required_supporting_findings: Radiographic evidence of completed endodontic treatment.
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).what_would_change_diagnosis: If canals are only partially treated/not obturated, use previously initiated therapy.
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).common_mistake_to_avoid: Calling it necrotic when the pulp has already been removed/treated.

Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).name: Previously Initiated Therapy
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).definition: A clinical diagnostic category indicating that the tooth has previously received partial endodontic therapy, such as pulpotomy or pulpectomy.
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).required_supporting_findings: History or radiographic/clinical evidence of partial endodontic therapy.
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).what_would_change_diagnosis: If fully obturated, use previously treated.
Pulp Diagnosis (AAE).common_mistake_to_avoid: Interpreting pulp tests normally when partial therapy may make responses unreliable.

diagnosticRules.name: Normal apical tissues
diagnosticRules.main_finding_pattern: No pain to percussion/palpation/biting and normal apical radiograph
diagnosticRules.confirming_findings: Uniform PDL space; intact lamina dura; no swelling or sinus tract.
diagnosticRules.do_not_confuse_with_note: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis with normal apical tissues can still have thermal pain. The apical diagnosis remains normal if apical tests are normal.

diagnosticRules.name: Symptomatic apical periodontitis
diagnosticRules.main_finding_pattern: Pain to biting, percussion, and/or palpation; radiograph may be normal or abnormal ("Widened PDL", "Radiolucency")
diagnosticRules.confirming_findings: Reproducible tenderness to percussion, palpation, or bite test.
diagnosticRules.do_not_confuse_with_note: Acute apical abscess if swelling/pus/systemic signs are present; cracked tooth if bite/release pattern and isolated probing suggest fracture.

diagnosticRules.name: Asymptomatic apical periodontitis
diagnosticRules.main_finding_pattern: Apical radiolucency but no pain to percussion or palpation
diagnosticRules.confirming_findings: Radiographic apical bone destruction of pulpal origin, clinically asymptomatic.
diagnosticRules.do_not_confuse_with_note: Chronic apical abscess if a draining sinus tract is present; non-endodontic radiolucencies if pulpal origin is not confirmed.

diagnosticRules.name: Chronic apical abscess
diagnosticRules.main_finding_pattern: Sinus tract, parulis, or intermittent drainage with little/no discomfort
diagnosticRules.confirming_findings: Gutta-percha tracing points to involved root/tooth; radiolucency commonly present.
diagnosticRules.do_not_confuse_with_note: Periodontal abscess, vertical root fracture, or acute apical abscess with active swelling/pain.

diagnosticRules.name: Acute apical abscess
diagnosticRules.main_finding_pattern: Rapid onset spontaneous pain + swelling/pus + extreme tenderness to pressure
diagnosticRules.confirming_findings: Localized or diffuse swelling; possible fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy; radiograph may be normal early.
diagnosticRules.do_not_confuse_with_note: Symptomatic apical periodontitis without swelling; chronic apical abscess with a draining sinus and minimal pain.

diagnosticRules.name: Condensing osteitis
diagnosticRules.main_finding_pattern: Periapical radiopacity/sclerosis associated with an endodontic inflammatory source
diagnosticRules.confirming_findings: Diffuse radiopaque apical lesion; often deep caries/large restoration/necrotic or chronically inflamed pulp.
diagnosticRules.do_not_confuse_with_note: Idiopathic osteosclerosis, cemento-osseous dysplasia, hypercementosis, anatomic radiopacity.

diagnosticRules.name: Acute apical abscess possible with normal radiograph
diagnosticRules.most_likely_periapical_diagnosis: Acute apical abscess is still possible
diagnosticRules.main_finding_pattern: Radiograph is normal but patient has severe pressure tenderness and swelling
diagnosticRules.confirming_findings: AAE notes acute apical abscess may have no radiographic signs of destruction.
diagnosticRules.do_not_confuse_with_note: Do not downgrade to normal apical tissues only because the radiograph is normal.

diagnosticRules.name: Radiolucency with painful percussion
diagnosticRules.most_likely_periapical_diagnosis: Symptomatic apical periodontitis, unless abscess signs are present
diagnosticRules.main_finding_pattern: Radiograph shows apical radiolucency but percussion is painful
diagnosticRules.confirming_findings: Pain to percussion/palpation makes the apical lesion symptomatic.
diagnosticRules.do_not_confuse_with_note: Asymptomatic apical periodontitis requires no clinical symptoms; acute abscess requires swelling/pus/rapid onset.

clinicalDiagnosticSummaryTable.summary_rule_or_definition: Select one pulpal diagnosis and one periapical diagnosis for the tooth.
No pain to percussion or palpation; intact lamina dura and uniform periodontal ligament space.
Pain on biting and/or percussion or palpation; may or may not have apical radiolucency.
Apical radiolucency/destruction of apical periodontium of pulpal origin, without clinical symptoms.
Rapid onset, spontaneous pain, tenderness to pressure, pus formation, and swelling associated with pulpal infection/necrosis.
Gradual onset, little or no discomfort, and intermittent pus discharge through a sinus tract associated with pulpal infection/necrosis.
Diffuse radiopaque lesion at the apex caused by localized bone reaction to low-grade inflammatory stimulus.
If pulp tests truly normal/vital, do not automatically assign pulpal-origin apical periodontitis; consider non-endodontic causes or limitations of tests.
Periapical diagnoses remain possible because signs may reflect persistent/recurrent infection, incomplete treatment, or healing status.

clinicalAssessmentsAndTests.positive_abnormal_result_suggests: Biting pain suggests symptomatic apical periodontitis; rapid swelling and spontaneous pain suggests acute apical abscess; intermittent gum boil/drainage suggests chronic apical abscess.
Visible swelling or sinus tract strongly affects the apical diagnosis. Cracks/restorations may explain bite pain or endodontic infection.
Pain/tenderness indicates inflammation of the periodontal ligament/apical tissues, not pulp vitality.
Tenderness may indicate extension of apical inflammation through cortical bone/periosteal tissues.
Pain to biting/pressure supports symptomatic apical periodontitis; pain on release may suggest a crack that needs separate evaluation.
Tracing to the apex or root identifies the endodontic source of drainage.

Apical radiolucency supports asymptomatic apical periodontitis/chronic abscess; radiopacity supports condensing osteitis; normal radiograph does not exclude symptomatic apical periodontitis or acute apical abscess.
Determines the separate pulpal diagnosis that must be paired with the periapical diagnosis.
Isolated deep narrow probing may suggest vertical root fracture or periodontal-endodontic lesion; generalized deep pockets may point to periodontal disease.

clinicalAssessmentsAndTests.positive_abnormal_result_suggests: Fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy, spreading swelling, or airway risk increases urgency and may affect medical management.
